reason: The passage uses 'evaluations' for tests of AI agents in general; the candidates are all narrower kinds (human, pairwise, listwise, pointwise, tool call), so none is the general idea.
'AI agents' here means LLM-based systems that use tools and act over many turns, which is the agentic system candidate's definition; agent loop is only the cycle they run.
'Evals' is the short form of evaluations in general; every candidate is a narrower type of evaluation or a specific framework.
The passage defines an evaluation as a test of an AI system with grading logic, the general concept; the candidates are specific subtypes.
'eval' is defined in the passage as the short form of evaluation, the general concept; no candidate is that general idea, and OpenAI and MAJ-EVAL are unrelated.
Automated evals are evals run without real users during development; the candidates are narrower deterministic-check evaluation types, so none is this broader category.
Single-turn evaluations are a prompt, a response and grading logic; pointwise evaluation scores one output but is a different axis (scoring style, not number of turns), so it is not the same idea.
'LLMs' means large language models in general; no candidate is that concept (LLM-as-a-judge is one use of them).
Multi-turn evaluations assess interactions of several turns; none of the candidates (scoring or comparison styles) covers that.
Agent evaluations assess agents that use tools across many turns and modify state; no candidate is evaluation of agents as a whole (tool input evaluation is only one aspect).
Here a task is a single test with defined inputs and success criteria in an eval; none of the bias or scale candidates relates to it.
The passage gives 'test case' as another name for an evaluation task; no candidate covers it.
A trial is one attempt at an evaluation task, repeated to handle output variance; no candidate matches.
A grader is logic that scores part of an agent's performance; a rubric is a set of criteria a grader may use, not the grader itself.
A transcript is the complete record of a trial including outputs and tool calls; none of the candidates is that record (LangSmith is a tool, not the concept).
The passage says trace is another name for a transcript, the full record of a trial; no candidate matches.
The passage says trajectory is another name for a transcript, the full record of a trial; no candidate matches.
The Anthropic API is a particular product of the company, not the company Anthropic itself; no candidate is the API.
An evaluation harness is the infrastructure that runs evals end-to-end; none of the candidates is that.
An agent harness is the system that lets a model act as an agent; the agent loop is only the cycle it runs and an agentic system is the whole built thing, so neither is the same.
The passage gives scaffold as another name for an agent harness; control flow and the other candidates are different ideas.
Claude Code is a named Anthropic agent product, used here as an example agent harness; no candidate is it.
The Agent SDK is a named Anthropic toolkit for building agents on Claude Code's primitives; no candidate is it.
An evaluation suite is a collection of tasks measuring specific capabilities; no candidate is that collection.
'eval suite' is the passage's short form of evaluation suite, a collection of tasks; no candidate matches.
Dogfooding means a team using its own product internally; none of the candidates covers it.
Production monitoring is observing a deployed system's behaviour in live use; regression testing and the other candidates are different ideas.
A/B tests compare two variants on real use, which is the A/B testing candidate's definition; the mention is its plural form.
Edge cases are unusual inputs or situations a spec may not cover; none of the candidates is that idea.
Baselines here are reference measurements (latency, cost, error rates) tracked over time; none of the candidates, including reference-based evaluation, is that.
Regression tests are tests re-run to check earlier behaviour has not worsened, the same idea as the regression testing candidate in plural form.
Code-based graders are one of three grader types, graders that use code to check output; no candidate is that, and reference-based evaluation is a different axis.

Model-based graders use a model to score outputs, which overlaps with LLM judging, but no LLM-as-a-judge candidate is offered, and the listed ones (panel of judges, reference-based evaluation) are narrower.
Capability or quality evals ask what an agent can do well and start at low pass rates; none of the candidates is that evaluation type.
Regression evals are evals expected to pass nearly always to detect backsliding; regression testing is the general practice, so this is a narrower evaluation kind and a match is not safe.
'capability evals' refers to the evals that ask what the agent can do well; no candidate matches.
A regression suite is a collection of tasks run continuously to catch drift, a set of tests rather than the practice of regression testing; the match is doubtful so it is treated as new.
Coding agents are LLM agents that write and modify code; the candidates cover generic agent loops, judges and a leaderboard, not this kind of agent.
Deterministic graders score outputs by fixed pass-or-fail checks such as running tests; none of the candidates is this grader type.
SWE-bench Verified is a named benchmark for coding agents; no candidate is a benchmark.
Terminal-Bench is named as a widely used coding agent benchmark; none of the candidates is a benchmark.
Conversational agents are a type of tool-using agent whose interaction quality is evaluated; no candidate covers this.
The passage uses rubrics in the general sense of criteria for grading task completion and interaction quality, matching the rubric candidate and its plural.
LLM here means the language model that simulates the user; none of the candidates is the general concept of a large language model.
tau-Bench is a named benchmark of simulated multi-turn user-agent interactions; no candidate is a benchmark.
tau2-Bench is the named successor to tau-Bench, a different benchmark version, and no candidate is a benchmark.
Research agents are a kind of agent that gathers and synthesizes information; the candidates cover agent loops and agentic systems generally, which are broader.
Groundedness checks verify that claims are supported by retrieved sources, which none of the candidates describes.
Coverage checks test whether an answer includes key required facts, which no candidate covers.
Source quality checks confirm that consulted sources are authoritative; authority bias is a different concept about judges.
LLM-based rubrics are rubrics applied by a model grader, narrower than the general rubric and distinct from LLM-as-a-judge itself; I do not match.
pass@k is defined in the passage as the likelihood of at least one correct solution in k attempts; no candidate is a metric of this kind.
pass@1 is the k=1 case of pass@k, success on the first attempt; no candidate matches.
The mention names a practice of defining success early and iterating on evals; no candidate describes it.
The 80/20 approach is the Pareto principle applied to starting with a small set of tasks for most of the value.

A reference solution is a known-working output proving a task is solvable and graders are configured; it resembles reference response but serves a different purpose, and the passage does not settle it.

Class-imbalanced refers to datasets with skewed class proportions; no candidate covers this.
Claude.ai is Anthropic's chat product, a particular tool, not the Anthropic organisation or any listed candidate.
Undertriggering means failing to perform a behaviour such as searching when it should; no candidate covers this.
Overtriggering means performing a behaviour such as searching when it should not; no candidate covers this.
An eval harness is the infrastructure that runs agent trials in isolated environments; the candidates are unrelated.
LLM graders are model-based graders, and the passage itself equates them with LLM-as-judge graders, matching the first candidate.
Human graders are people grading for validation, close to both human evaluation and human review, and the passage does not choose between them.
Partial credit means scoring multi-component tasks on a continuum rather than pass/fail; no candidate matches.
Transcripts here are the recorded agent trial logs read to check graders; no candidate covers them.
Eval saturation is defined in the passage as an agent passing all solvable tasks, leaving no room for improvement; no candidate matches.
An evaluation suite is a maintained collection of evals; none of the candidates describes this.
Unit tests are the software testing practice used as an analogy; none of the candidates is that.
Eval-driven development means writing evals for planned capabilities before building them; no candidate matches.
Automated evaluations are evals run by code or models at scale; the candidates are specific eval types or human evaluation, which is the opposite.
User feedback is signal from real users about a product; no candidate covers it, and RLHF is a different thing.
Manual transcript review is people reading agent transcripts; it is narrower than human review, so I do not match.
Systematic human evaluation is human evaluation done in a structured way, matching the candidate.
CI/CD is the software practice of continuous integration and delivery; no candidate is related.
Distribution drift is a shift in real-world input data over time; no candidate covers it.
Transcript review is people reading agent transcripts, narrower than human review, so I do not match.
Systematic human studies used to calibrate graders with human consensus as the reference are human evaluation.
The Swiss Cheese Model is a safety-engineering model of layered defences; none of the candidates is that.
